query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning–based predictive approach that employs transferable features derived from binary and ternary alloy data to capture local chemical and force constant fluctuations in high-entropy alloys will more accurately identify compositions with extremely low phonon (lattice) thermal conductivity compared with current scattering‐models that assume increasing disorder necessarily results in higher phonon attenuation.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloys with a random distribution of 5 or more elements (e.g., FeCoCrMnNi) showing inherent lattice distortions and established force-constant fluctuations (~20–50%).
generation.intervention: Apply the ML model trained on binary/ternary alloys to predict the degree of force constant fluctuations and consequent phonon scattering in HEAs, then select candidate alloys predicted to have ultra-low phonon thermal conductivity.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under controlled synthesis yielding uniform, single-phase HEA samples; phonon properties measured at room and low temperatures using inelastic scattering (or similar) techniques.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical fluctuations and lattice distortions that induce force constant variations, which in turn enhance phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: The approach works by recognizing that the key mediator for low thermal conductivity in HEAs is not merely the increased number of elements, but how local environments modulate force constant fluctuations. By using features from simpler systems, the ML model accurately captures these fluctuations and correlates them to reduced phonon lifetimes and lower thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predictive model should identify HEA compositions that exhibit a lower lattice thermal conductivity (for example, achieving values near or below those measured in benchmark HEAs like FeCoCrMnNi, e.g., ~10 W/mK or less for the phonon contribution) with improved accuracy over conventional models.
generation.baseline: Current scattering-based approaches, such as those following Mu’s theory, typically predict increased phonon attenuation with the assumed higher variability in multi-component systems, which does not align with some experimental observations (e.g., similar phonon conductivity values between binary and multi-element alloys).
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to apply only to single-phase, homogeneous HEAs with random elemental distributions. It may not be valid for multiphase alloys or systems with significant elemental segregation where the training data from binary systems become non-transferable.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in prediction accuracy is uncertain, as is the degree to which binary/ternary training data can be reliably extrapolated to more complex HEA systems. Further empirical validation is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize several single-phase HEAs with varying compositions as predicted by the ML model. Measure their phonon dispersion relations via inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering and determine their lattice thermal conductivity using an independent method such as time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) at room and low temperatures. Compare the experimental thermal conductivities with the ML predictions and with those predicted by traditional scattering models.
measurements: Force constant fluctuation estimates (via scattering attenuation data)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across multiple HEA compositions, the experimentally determined lattice thermal conductivity deviates by more than approximately 20% from the model predictions—or if the ML approach does not demonstrate a clear accuracy improvement over conventional phonon scattering models—the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, entropy engineering has been used as a novel strategy to optimize the electrical and thermal transport properties of TE materials. By increasing element species, the mixing entropy in a material system increases quickly, and high-entropy materials with over five principal elements will be formed. Severe lattice distortion is usually the core phenomenon of high-entropy material—such distortion leads to strong scattering for heat-carrying phonons and results in low lattice thermal conductivity. Stabilizing single-phase structures by increasing entropy weakens the phase-boundary electron scattering in multiphase high-entropy material, thus providing a beneficial contribution to improve electrical transport properties, i.e., entropy-driven structural stabilization,. Therefore, the high-entropy-stabilized composition should work as a good matrix for further optimization of TE performance by integrating the traditional optimization strategy.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. If this is unexpected from Mu’s theory, which would predict increased force-constant fluctuations due to the larger variability of random environments of a given atomic pair, it explains recent experimental reports on comparable phonon lattice thermal conductivities in our HEA and FeNi

cited_evidence.text: Using the same approach, the value of κL was computed for various temperatures in the range 300–700 K (Figure 9). At 300 K, the κL value is 0.4 W K−1 m−1, which is a very low value of the lattice thermal conductivity, favorable for thermoelectric materials. This is due to the lattice distortion effect of high-entropy alloys that can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low thermal conductivity. Additionally, one can observe that when the temperature rises, the thermal conductivity of the lattice decreases, which is also due to an increase in phonon scattering at higher temperatures.
